opus-5.5.text:
For me, the most interesting part is that the web was built for humans, and we're trying to rebuild the core of it for a different kind of user. When a person searches, they want ten links, they skim, they click, and they bring their own judgment. An agent wants something else. It wants the right tokens in its context window, with enough evidence to reason over, and it wants that reliably at very high volume.

That changes the technical problem at almost every layer. On the index side, you're not just ranking pages for click-through. You're asking which passages from which sources, at what freshness, actually answer what the agent is trying to do. So you end up thinking about retrieval in terms of information density per token rather than relevance per link.

Then there's the compute dimension, which I find really exciting. With human search, latency dominates everything because a person is waiting. With agents, some tasks need an answer in a second, while others are deep research tasks where it's fine to spend minutes and a lot more compute if the result is substantially better. So we think of it as a spectrum where you let the developer choose how much work the system does, and the quality should scale with that. Building the system so that more compute reliably buys you more accuracy is a hard and fun problem.

The third piece is verifiability. If an agent is going to act on what it found, it needs to know how confident to be. So attaching citations, provenance, and calibrated confidence to outputs, rather than just returning text, is something we care a lot about. Agents compound errors across many steps, so a small improvement in grounding at the search layer pays off disproportionately downstream.

And underneath all of it is evaluation. The tasks people give agents are open-ended and long-tailed, so building benchmarks that actually reflect real workloads, and being honest about where we're good and where we aren't, ends up driving a lot of the technical roadmap.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I'd frame it is that the interesting work isn't really "search" in the sense people are used to. Web search as we've known it was built for humans: you type a few words, you get ten links, you do the reading, the synthesis, the judgment. The product was optimized for a person sitting in front of a screen with a limited attention budget.

Agents are a completely different consumer. They don't want ten links. They want the answer, with evidence, and they're willing to spend a lot more compute to get it right. So the first thing we had to rethink is the shape of the interface. An agent asks a question, not a keyword query, and it often wants structured output, not a ranked list. That changes what the system underneath has to do.

The technical core, to me, is in three places.

One is the retrieval layer. If you're going to serve agents, you need an index that's built for machines to read, not for humans to skim. That means going much deeper into the long tail of the web, keeping pages fresh, and representing content in a way that a model can actually reason over rather than just matching tokens. A lot of the web's value is in pages no human would ever click on from a results page, but which are exactly what an agent needs to verify a fact.

Two is the agentic loop itself. A hard question usually can't be answered with one retrieval. You have to decompose it, run multiple searches, read the sources, notice contradictions, go back and look again. We spend a lot of time on how to orchestrate that: when to go wider, when to go deeper, when to stop. And that has to be tunable, because sometimes the caller wants a fast, cheap answer and sometimes they want something closer to a research report. Exposing that as a dial, in a way that's actually predictable for the developer, is harder than it sounds.

Three, and this is the one I find most interesting, is calibration. If an agent is going to act on what you return, it needs to know how much to trust it. So we attach confidence and citations to every claim, and we work hard to make sure those confidence scores actually mean something, that a ninety-percent-confidence answer is right about ninety percent of the time. The failure mode you really want to avoid is a system that sounds equally sure whether it's right or wrong. Getting that honest signal out of a system that's itself built on models is a real research problem, and it's the thing that makes the output usable in a pipeline rather than just impressive in a demo.

And then underneath all of that is the economics. Agents issue orders of magnitude more queries than humans, and each one can involve a lot more work. So the engineering challenge is doing all of this at a cost that lets people actually build on it. That's where a lot of the unglamorous but important work lives.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting technical work is in asking what search should look like when the consumer is an agent. A person can look at a page of links, click around, and decide what’s useful. An agent needs to do that as part of a larger task, so the interface has to help it find evidence, understand it, and decide whether it has enough information to move forward.

That makes this more than a retrieval problem. How do you break a complex question into searches? When do you go deeper on a source, and when do you look for another one? How do you preserve the connection between an answer and the evidence behind it?

And then there’s the tradeoff between quality, latency, and cost. You can keep searching, but at some point the next search isn’t helping enough. Figuring out how to make those decisions—and measuring whether they actually help the agent complete its task—is where I see a lot of the interesting work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting technical work starts with asking what search should look like when the consumer is an agent rather than a person. A person can look at ten links, click around, and decide what’s useful. An agent needs information it can reason over, with enough context and evidence to take the next step reliably.

That changes the problem. You’re optimizing not just for whether a result looks relevant, but for whether it helps the agent complete its task. What information is missing? Should you search again? Which sources support a particular claim? When do you have enough evidence to stop?

And then there’s the systems challenge of doing that within a useful latency and cost budget. You can spend more time exploring and checking, but you need to know when that additional work actually improves the answer. I find that intersection—retrieval, reasoning, and deciding where to spend computation—particularly interesting.
